explain.say: Have you seen someone push, fold and squash bread dough for ages? That's called kneading, and it isn't just for fun! Look at the first stage. Wheat flour has two hidden proteins, and when you add water, they start to wake up.

explain.say: See the wire at the next stage? The wet proteins join into long, stretchy strands called gluten. At first they're a tangled mess, like a pile of loose string. Can you think of anything else that's stretchy?

explain.say: Now look at the hand. Kneading pulls and folds the dough again and again, lining up the gluten strands into a strong, springy net. Well-kneaded dough stretches so thin you can almost see light through it, without tearing!

explain.say: See the bubbles? Tiny living yeast eats sugar in the dough and gives off a gas, carbon dioxide. The gluten net catches the gas like millions of tiny balloons, so the dough puffs up. Why do you think unkneaded dough stays flatter?

faq.a: Gluten is a stretchy network made when two wheat proteins, glutenin and gliadin, mix with water. It gives dough its springy feel.
asks: What does gluten do in bread?

faq.a: Kneading lines up the gluten strands into a strong, stretchy net. That net traps the gas from yeast, so the bread rises and is light.

faq.q: How do you know when dough is kneaded enough?
faq.a: It turns smooth and springy. Bakers use the windowpane test: stretch a small piece thin, and if light shows through without it tearing, it's ready.

faq.q: What happens if you don't knead bread?
faq.a: The gluten net stays weak, so it can't hold much gas, and the bread comes out flat and dense. No-knead recipes use a long, slow rest to build the net instead.
asks: Can you make bread without kneading?

faq.a: Without gluten there is no stretchy net, so gluten-free breads use eggs, gums or seeds to trap the bubbles instead. People with coeliac disease must avoid gluten.

facts: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin are mixed with water.
Yeast makes bread rise by giving off carbon dioxide gas as it feeds on sugars.
